title: Null Safety & Optional Types
summary: Tony Hoare's billion-dollar mistake and how modern type systems eliminate null-pointer bugs at compile time by making absence an explicit, checked part of the type itself.

slides.markdown:
Two Topics ago, this group's pitfall on static typing named `NullPointerException` as proof that static typing doesn't mean crash-free — a legally typed `String` can still be `null`, and dereferencing it crashes at runtime despite the program compiling cleanly. This Topic is the fix for exactly that hole.

Tony Hoare, who invented the null reference in 1965, later called it his **"billion-dollar mistake"** — not because null is a bad concept, but because most type systems let *every* reference type silently include null as a valid value, with no way to tell from a type signature alone whether a given value can actually be absent.

The fix modern languages converge on: make absence an explicit, checked *type*, not a hidden possibility every reference secretly carries. Once absence is in the type, the compiler can force you to handle it — the bug doesn't disappear from reality, but it moves from a runtime crash to a compile-time requirement to deal with it.

slides.subTitle: Why it's a type-system problem
slides.markdown:
Hoare's own framing matters: he didn't say null itself was a mistake — representing "this value is absent" is a genuinely necessary concept. His mistake, in his words, was making it possible "simply because it was so easy to implement," with no separate checking, so that *every* reference type in a null-permissive language secretly includes an extra hidden value (null) that behaves nothing like the type's declared members.

The consequence is specifically a type-system failure, not a logic-error problem in general: a `String` parameter's type signature promises you'll get a `String` — something with `.length()`, `.substring()`, all the real `String` behavior — but the type says nothing about whether you might instead get null, which has none of that behavior and crashes on contact with any of it. The type lied about what values are actually possible, and the type checker, having been told `String`, has no way to warn you that a `null` might show up instead.

This framing — "the type promised something it didn't actually guarantee" — is the precise reason this is a type-system problem, fixable by changing what types can express, rather than just a discipline problem fixable by "being more careful."

slides.sectionTitle: A nullable reference sneaking past the checker
slides.markdown:
Trace a `String` value from a function that can return null, through a type checker that has no concept of nullability, to a crash.

`findUser(id)` is declared to return `String` (the user's name), but its actual implementation returns `null` when no user matches `id` — nothing in the `String` return type prevents this. The caller, `String name = findUser(id); System.out.println(name.length());`, compiles cleanly: the type checker sees a `String` flowing into a `String`-typed variable, matching perfectly, with no signal anywhere that this particular `String` might secretly be absent.

The crash happens at `name.length()`, at runtime, only when `findUser` actually returns null for some `id` — which might be a rare edge case that doesn't show up until production traffic hits it. The type checker approved every step of this path; the bug was invisible to it because the type `String` never distinguished "definitely a string" from "a string, or possibly nothing."

slides.subTitle: Making absence explicit and checked
slides.markdown:
The fix: instead of letting every `T` secretly also mean "or nothing," wrap the possibility of absence in its own distinct type — `Option<T>` (Rust, Scala) or `Maybe<T>` (Haskell) — which is *not* the same type as `T` itself. A function that might not have a value to return has to say so in its signature: `findUser(id: string): Option<User>`, not `findUser(id: string): User`.

The payoff is entirely mechanical, not a matter of discipline: `Option<User>` has no `.name` field directly accessible — you cannot call a `User`-specific method on it without first checking whether it actually holds a value. The type system itself forces the check, at the type level, before any `User`-specific operation is legal, which is a completely different guarantee from "the `User`-typed value might secretly be null and you should remember to check."

This is the core idea the rest of this Topic elaborates on: absence stops being an invisible extra state every reference silently carries, and becomes a real, distinct, checkable type that the compiler enforces you handle before you can get at the value underneath.

Kotlin, Swift, and TypeScript's strict mode take a different, arguably cleaner approach to the same problem: rather than wrapping optionality in a separate generic type, they make **every plain type non-nullable by default**, and require an explicit marker (`String?` in Kotlin/TypeScript, `String?` in Swift) to opt a specific type into allowing null at all.

`fun greet(name: String)` in Kotlin genuinely cannot receive null — the compiler rejects `greet(null)` at the call site, full stop, because `String` (unmarked) excludes null by the type system's own rule, not by convention. If a function needs to accept an absent name, its signature has to say so explicitly: `fun greet(name: String?)`, and the compiler then forces a null check (`if (name != null)`, or the `?.`/`?:` operators) before any `String`-specific method can be called on `name` inside that function.

The practical difference from `Optional<T>`: there's no separate wrapper type to unwrap — `String?` is still fundamentally a `String`, just one the compiler additionally tracks as possibly-null, and the checks (`?.`, `?:`, smart-cast after an `if (name != null)`) are built into the language's core syntax rather than living in a library type's methods.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: .get() without a check just moves the crash
slides.markdown:
Adopting `Optional<T>` doesn't automatically eliminate null-pointer-style bugs — it's entirely possible to write `optional.get()` without ever checking `.isPresent()` first, and if the `Optional` is actually empty, `.get()` throws `NoSuchElementException` at exactly that line. This is functionally the same crash as the `NullPointerException` it was meant to replace, just with a different exception name and, crucially, the exact same failure to actually check.

This happens most often when a developer treats `Optional` as a hoop to jump through rather than a genuine safety mechanism — wrapping a return type in `Optional<T>` to satisfy an API convention, then immediately calling `.get()` at every call site out of habit, defeating the entire point. The type system *permits* this because `.get()` is a legal method on `Optional` — it can't stop you from calling it unsafely, it can only make the safe alternative (`.map()`/`.orElse()`, or an explicit `isPresent()` check) available and idiomatic.

The accurate framing for this pitfall: `Optional<T>` (and nullable types generally) give the *type system the vocabulary* to express and check absence — they don't force good usage on their own. Code review and linting (many teams ban unchecked `.get()` calls outright) are what actually close this remaining gap.

| | Null-permissive (Java, loose TypeScript) | Null-safe-by-default (Kotlin, Swift, Rust) |
|---|---|---|
| **Default nullability** | Every reference type can be null unless otherwise proven | Every type excludes null unless explicitly marked (`T?`) or wrapped (`Option<T>`) |
| **Compiler catches missing null checks?** | No — nullability isn't tracked in the type system at all | Yes — dereferencing a nullable value without a check is a compile error |
| **Migration cost for existing code** | None — this is the historical default | Real — retrofitting an existing null-permissive codebase requires auditing every reference for actual nullability |

The migration-cost row explains why null-permissive languages haven't simply switched defaults: Java's entire existing ecosystem assumes any reference *might* be null, and changing that default would break assumptions baked into decades of code, libraries, and APIs — which is why Java instead added optional, non-default tools (`Optional<T>`, `@Nullable` annotations checked by external tools) rather than changing what a plain `String` means.

slides.sectionTitle: Redesign this API so null bugs are impossible
slides.markdown:
This exact prompt — redesign an API to make null bugs impossible, not just less likely — tests whether you reach for the type-level fix rather than a discipline-based one.

A weak answer adds a comment ("// may return null, check before using") or a `@Nullable` annotation that a linter can flag but the compiler can't enforce — both rely on every future caller remembering to check, which is exactly the discipline-based approach that got the industry a billion dollars of bugs in the first place.

A strong answer changes the *type* so an unchecked usage cannot compile: `findUser(id: string): User` — which lies about nullability if the implementation can return nothing — becomes `findUser(id: string): Option<User>` (or `User?` in a null-safe-by-default language). Now every caller is *forced* by the compiler to handle the absent case before they can reach any `User`-specific member, not just encouraged to remember it. The redesign doesn't make the underlying reality (a user might not exist) go away — it makes the compiler the enforcer of handling that reality, instead of relying on every caller's memory.

The unifying idea across `Optional<T>`, Kotlin's `T?`, and Rust's `Option<T>`: absence is real and unavoidable in software (a lookup can fail, a field can be unset), and the only question is whether your *type system* knows about it. When it doesn't, absence is a hidden extra state every reference secretly carries, discovered only at the crash site. When it does, absence becomes an explicit type the compiler forces every caller to confront before proceeding.

This Topic closes out the practical, everyday half of the group's advanced material — the last Topic, algebraic data types, generalizes this exact idea past just "present or absent" to *any* fixed set of alternative shapes a value might take, of which `Option<T>` (present or absent — exactly two cases) turns out to be the simplest possible example.
